<div class="accordion" id="workAccordion">
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-author">Author</button></h2><div id="work-acc-author" class="accordion-collapse collapse show"><div class="accordion-body"><p class="mb-0 work-author"><a href="../poets/damodaragupta.html">Dāmodaragupta / दामोदरगुप्त</a></p></div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-summary">Summary</button></h2><div id="work-acc-summary" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Dāmodaragupta's Kuṭṭanīmata is a masterpiece of satirical, humorous literature with clear didactic goals which is written in “Āryā” metre. It also contains much information on life and culture of the early mediaeval Northern India. Kuṭṭanī is a term used to entitle a prostitute. Kuṭṭanīmata is a term used to understand and trace the characteristics and lifestyle of prostitutes through this poem. The story centres around a young Brahmin named Kuṭṭanī who is born into a family of scholars and priests. However, Kuṭṭanī is different from the other Brahmins in his community because he is a free spirit who loves to play practical jokes and mock the traditional rituals and customs of his people. As a result of his behaviour, Kuṭṭanī becomes an outcast in his community and is shunned by his family and friends. However, he finds solace in the company of a group of low-caste people who accept him for who he is. The play is a commentary on the social hierarchy of ancient India, which was based on the caste system. It critiques the idea that people should be judged by their birth rather than their actions and character.<br><br>Dāmodaragupta depicts a society dominated by the mercantile community with wealth concentrated in the hands of a few privileged individuals, including rājaputras, śreṣṭhis and vanikas. The high life revolves around them and is exclusive to them. The royal authority does not assert itself very much. Even petty officers in the state service can get away with misbehaving without caring too much about what action comes from the top. There is a solid attraction to wealth and attachment to the material luxuries of life. Prostitution is tolerated in society as a necessary evil and appears to receive a lot of benefaction. However, a young fellow is distressed by the act of the people, while he fell in love with a prostitute. <br>The wealthy mercantile and the high life of the princely class no doubt produces fine things in dress, ornaments, games and amusements, food and drink, and possibly arts and crafts that make life more enjoyable. But that is all there is to life, and it is confined to a small group at the top. If one looks for contributions made by the society as described and depicted in Dāmodaragupta's work to humanity in the realm of intellectual speculation, he is likely to be disappointed.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contents">Contents</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contents" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Kuṭṭanī-Mata is a poetry, where a greater number of verses being lost, 927 Ślokas (verses) are remaining in the text. There are few stories being inserted in the poetry, in order to bring more connectedness within the reader.  <br>The poem begins with Kuṭṭanī's birth into a family of Brahmin priests. As a child, Kuṭṭanī is different from other Brāhmaṇas  because he loves to play practical jokes and mock traditional customs. He is eventually shunned by his family and community and turns to a group of low-caste people for acceptance. Kuṭṭanī's rebellious nature leads him to challenge the caste system and the traditional roles of men and women. He argues that people should be judged by their actions and character rather than their birth, and he supports the rights of women to choose their own partners.<br><br>Kuṭṭanī's ideas are met with resistance from the conservative members of his society, who try to silence him through force and intimidation. However, Kuṭṭanī continues to advocate for social justice and individual freedom, and he ultimately becomes a heroic figure. The poem uses humour, satire, and irony to critique the oppressive social norms of ancient Indian society and to celebrate the power of individuality and freedom. It is a significant work of Sanskrit literature and has influenced many later writers and thinkers in India.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-uniqueness">Uniqueness</button></h2><div id="work-acc-uniqueness" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">The work Kuṭṭanī-Mata exhibits the liberal nature of a young fellow in the 8th century AD. This shows that the society although sought to be traditional in its approach, had various kinds of people back then like it is in the present day. Also, it is to be noted that, Sanskrit literature is not only meant for conventional writing, but also the liberal thinkers existed at those times. Dāmodaragupta is one good example.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contribution">Contribution &amp; Notes</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contribution" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">&quot;Kuṭṭanī-Mata&quot; is considered to be a significant work of Sanskrit literature due to its contribution to the development of Sanskrit poetry and its exploration of social and philosophical themes. Here are some ways in which the poem has contributed to Sanskrit literature:<br>Poetic Techniques: The poem uses a variety of poetic techniques, including similes, metaphors, allusions, and wordplay. These techniques demonstrate the richness and complexity of Sanskrit poetry and have influenced later poets and writers.<br>Social Commentary: &quot;Kuṭṭanī-Mata&quot; is a commentary on the oppressive social norms of ancient Indian society, including the caste system, gender roles, and the treatment of outcasts. The poem critiques these norms and advocates for social justice and individual freedom.<br>Philosophical Exploration: The poem also explores philosophical themes such as the nature of reality, the role of the individual in society, and the meaning of life. These explorations demonstrate the depth and complexity of Sanskrit literature and its engagement with important philosophical questions.<br><br>&quot;Kuṭṭanī-Mata&quot; is written in the &quot;āryā&quot; meter, which has 19 syllables in each line. This meter is known for its rhythmic complexity and is often used in Sanskrit poetry to convey philosophical or spiritual ideas. The poem is notable for its critique of the social and cultural norms of ancient Indian society and its emphasis on individual freedom and self-expression. It is also known for its use of allegory and metaphor to explore complex philosophical ideas, making it an important work of Sanskrit literature that continues to be studied and appreciated today.</div></div></div>
